transcript:
Meeting header
- Date/Time: 2026-08-11 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~58 mins
- Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood Solutions Eng), Marta (CTO - Palisade), Samir (Staff ML Eng), Alice (Infra Lead), Devon (SRE)

AUTO-SUMMARY (auto gen, may be incomplete): intermittent p99 bursts on hosted endpoints during business hours. Customer sees streaming responses sometimes degrade. Possible root causes discussed: network topology, KV cache hot keys, batch sizing, quantization tail effects. Next steps and action items captured.

00:00:02 Jared: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we know Palisade has been seeing these intermittent p99 spikes, so today Priya and I wanted to walk through lifecycle — err sorry, runtime traces and topology and try to reproduce.
00:00:12 Marta: thanks, yeah we've been waking up to alerts, mostly between 11:30 and 13:30 EST, p95 fine but p99 jumps a lot, like from 240ms to 1.8s for some requests.
00:00:25 Priya: okay, quick clarifying q, are the slow ones all streaming responses or both streaming and non-streaming?
00:00:30 Samir: mostly streaming chat completions, token-by-token output. non-streaming batch calls are mostly stable, though one-off spikes happened too.
00:00:38 Lena: do you have an example trace where you correlate token-throttle with network hop?
00:00:45 Samir: i'll upload a sample trace after this meeting, but just to confirm network wise we have a mesh between three VPCs and a NAT egress via a partner transit. so some calls traverse 3 hops.
00:00:58 Devon: also worth noting we do OBSN logs (flow logs) and sometimes the egress gateway CPU saturates during bursts but it's sporadic.
00:01:10 Priya: ok, so three primary hypotheses: one, multi-hop VPC and NAT causing tail latency amplification; two, KV cache hotkeys causing micro-queuing on a single shard; three, streaming path in the runtime has extra synchronization or fallback behavior under resource pressure. we'll walk each.
00:01:30 Marta: great. i also want to confirm we prefer hosted for now but may try a private deployment if the economics/latency tradeoff is favorable.

00:05:02 Priya: first, kv cache. our runtime does prefix/KV caching of key-value past states. when hot keys concentrate on one shard that shard's GPU or process can become a bottleneck. we saw examples where a 1% of keys cause 40% of requests.
00:05:22 Samir: yeah our traffic is very bursty — a push notification campaign triggers many similar prompts. we might be hitting the same prompt template repeatedly.
00:05:30 Priya: can you confirm whether you pin model versions or use fallback variants?
00:05:35 Samir: pinned to redwood-encoder-v2 but we've allowed fallback to quantized variant for cost savings on lower tiers.
00:05:44 Priya: okay fallback to quantized could change kernel selection and occasionally alter execution time per token, though it's typically faster; but it can increase variance if the quantized kernel isn't as well warm.
00:06:10 Jared: also streaming vs non-streaming: streaming path keeps a token pump, flushes on each token, and depends on network ACKs and small writes; that exposes you to network jitter and extra syscalls. non-streaming batches tokens then returns a blob, which hides per-token jitter.
00:06:28 Martha: (laughs) martha?
00:06:30 Marta: yep, that's us. so streaming is our default for chat UI.
00:06:34 Priya: one more thing: our runtime will sometimes redirect streaming requests to a compatible variant (e.g., smaller sequence or different shard) under high load to maintain throughput — that can cause ephemeral routing jitter.
00:06:46 Alice: how does that redirection happen with VPC private endpoints? are there extra network hops to the control plane?
00:06:54 Priya: for Redwood Private with VPC peering, control plane signals happen over the peering connection; there are small grpc calls but most heavy traffic stays in-region. if you use transit via partner there can be additional NAT which adds 20-200ms depending on burst.
00:07:10 Devon: we do have an egress NAT to central logging; sometimes logs and inference egress compete for bandwidth. weird split brain with flow logs.

00:09:01 Priya: let's dig into KV metrics — Samir, can you run a hot-key histogram? we recommend returning a 95/99 percentile of key frequency so we can see concentration. ideally show shard distribution.
00:09:14 Samir: yes i can do that; our current exporter shows top keys but not the full histogram, i'll enrich it.
00:09:20 Priya: good, also please snapshot the runtime's cache hit ratio over the bursts — we saw in other customers when hit ratio dips below 70% tail jumps.
00:09:31 Jared: note: sometimes mis-transcriptions in our logs call it K-V cash, so watch for that in your grep.

00:12:05 Priya: next network — multi-hop VPC. when requests go through 2-3 NATs or cross AZ, you can get queued packet delays and TCP slow-start interactions. also NAT devices have conntrack tables that may thrash during bursts.
00:12:20 Alice: our NAT instances are t3-like ephemeral; we saw conntrack overrun warnings during last campaign.
00:12:27 Priya: that matches. we typically recommend a direct VPC peering (no NAT) for production low-tail deployments or at least dedicated NAT gateways with auto-scaling.
00:12:37 Marta: but direct peering has policy constraints with partner networks, how much does latency improve? give ballpark numbers.
00:12:44 Priya: we've measured 50-200ms improvement on p99 in multi-region meshes moving to peering and eliminating extra NAT hops. for some customers it halved their p99.

00:15:00 Jared: i want to touch batching — if you tune batch windows we can reduce per-token cost and smooth variance, but that increases median latency. question: is Palisade willing to trade some median for improved p99?
00:15:14 Marta: we'd accept a small median increase if p99 becomes predictable and stays under 500ms.
00:15:22 Priya: then we can propose a hybrid: small 15ms micro-batching plus streaming flush thresholds so that you get most of streaming latency but with fewer syscalls. this reduces jitter.
00:15:35 Samir: micro-batching sounds promising, how does that interact with KV cache? could it increase cache thrash?
00:15:42 Priya: it can increase simultaneous cache lookups per batch; but if sharding is good and hot keys are sharded round-robin or by consistent hashing, it's fine. the problem is single-shard hot keys.

00:18:40 Priya: quantization — Samir you mentioned fallback to a quantized variant. quant kernels often have less predictable tail behavior because they use different memory patterns and may trigger different cuBLAS/cuDNN code paths. sometimes quantized int8 kernels have lower mean but slightly heavier tail on certain sequence lengths.
00:18:59 Samir: we've seen that on one model, after switching to int8 we had lower token cost but two specific prompt lengths spiked occasionally.
00:19:06 Priya: yeah that can happen if the quantized kernel isn't vectorized for that sequence length causing extra kernels to run. runtime can select alternate kernels; we can surface kernel usage traces to you — that will show which kernel executed for each token step.

00:21:00 Lena: quick note about compilation and kernel selection: our runtime maintains a small kernel inventory per model and will pick based on seq length and device. if the device is busy we sometimes fall back to a more generic kernel which can add variance.
00:21:15 Devon: is there an observable metric to capture kernel fallbacks?
00:21:19 Priya: yes, kernel_event.log and a metric "kernel_selection_fallback_count" we can enable in debug mode — it's a bit noisy but telling.

00:24:10 Jared: let's talk about repro steps. For the controlled replay on Dedicated, we'll want: sample request traces (timestamps + payload hashes), the VPC topology, and your prometheus scrape config. We'll spin a dedicated pool with the same model + quant variant and run at-scale replay for 3 hours across the traffic profile window you saw.
00:24:28 Marta: can you mimic our NAT topology in the replay environment?
00:24:33 Priya: we can approximate network delays using tc/netem to inject hop latencies and packet reorder, but we can't fully replicate proprietary transit behavior. however most NAT conntrack effects are reproduced by simulating the extra NAT hop and its resource constraints.
00:24:49 Alice: that helps. if you can simulate conntrack exhaustion patterns, we can confirm it's the culprit.

00:27:50 Samir: also on sampling — our traces are PII redacted, but we can provide hashed prompt templates and timestamps. is that enough?
00:27:57 Priya: yes hashed payloads plus timing and response sizes are fine. payload content isn't necessary to reproduce KV hot keys because the keying is based on prompt fingerprints which you can provide as hashes.

00:30:00 (brief static noise)
00:30:12 Jared: i want to call out a common pattern we've seen: a burst that saturates a single RPC connection or a shard will cause a cascading backpressure where streaming flushes queue behind KV lock. That turns a 200ms op into an amplified 1-2s op for subsequent requests.
00:30:31 Devon: we see that in our traces, a single process has long tail and others are fine. is vertical autoscaling recommended?
00:30:36 Priya: yes, vertical or horizontal. for Dedicated we recommend autoscaling with shard-awareness — if one shard sees high cpu or GPU utilization we can auto-spin a second replica for that shard. your current config is uniform scaling which is slower to react.
00:30:53 Samir: shard-awareness sounds great, how fast does it typically spin up?
00:30:58 Priya: with warm pool and pre-warmed images you can get new replicas in 30-90s. without warm pool it may be 3+ minutes. warm pool is strongly recommended for low-tail SLOs.

00:34:10 Lena: another mitigation is cache prewarming for predicted keys — for campaign traffic you can pre-insert the prompt templates into the cache before the blast. that eliminates the initial stampede.
00:34:23 Samir: we can prewarm but our campaign list sometimes has a million variants; we can do top-10k though.
00:34:29 Priya: top-10k is often enough; the 80/20 rule tends to apply for prompts. also TTL tuning: short TTLs can cause churn under bursts. increase TTL slightly during campaigns.

00:37:00 Marta: about Private vs Hosted — what are the tradeoffs for our latency problem?
00:37:06 Jared: Private (VPC/on-prem) reduces network hops to our control plane and can eliminate NAT egress; Dedicated in-region with peering is the middle ground. Hosted is easiest but more exposure to routing across public egress depending on your network.
00:37:20 Alice: if we go Private, do we still get auto-updates and kernel optimizations?
00:37:24 Priya: yes, we push runtime updates to Private control planes via our secure channel; however some customers schedule update windows. kernel optimizations are handled similarly but you control when they go live.

00:40:10 Priya: a few quick diagnostics we need you to capture before the replay: tcpdump around the NAT during a burst, conntrack histogram export, kernel_selection_fallback_count, kv_shard_hit_ratio with top-keys, and the prometheus scrape intervals.
00:40:28 Samir: noted. we'll add kernel logging but keep it limited to avoid perf overhead. how verbose is kernel_event.log?
00:40:34 Priya: it's per-token and can be large; we recommend sampling: enable for 1-5% of requests and correlate timestamps. that gives us signals without heavy overhead.

00:43:50 Devon: curious — you mentioned streaming vs non-streaming flush thresholds; where is that configured?
00:43:55 Priya: on the runtime config you can set stream_flush_ms and stream_batch_size; defaults are conservative (flush immediately) but you can set flush_ms to 15-50ms depending on user experience tolerance.
00:44:07 Marta: what about SDK behavior — does the client need to change?
00:44:10 Jared: no, we support server-side micro-batching transparently. the SDK may observe slightly higher median but smoother p99.

00:46:30 Priya: note on telemetry: we'll instrument per-token latency percentiles and make a dashboard showing p50/p95/p99 for streaming vs non-streaming. we'll also add an endpoint-level metric for kv-localization-score (how concentrated keys are on shards).
00:46:46 Samir: kv-localization-score sounds helpful, please define it.
00:46:50 Priya: it's basically the Gini coefficient of key frequency across shards — 0 is uniform, 1 is all keys on one shard. values above 0.6 are concerning.
00:47:03 Samir: good metric.

00:49:20 Jared: last bit — fallback policies. we can configure automatic fallback to compatible model variants if a replica is overloaded, but that can change token timing. suggest we set a conservative fallback threshold and have canary routing for the first minute of a spike.
00:49:34 Marta: ok we want predictable behavior, so canary+graceful fallback makes sense.

00:52:00 Priya: to summarize action items: we'll run the 3-hour replay, enable sampled kernel logging, and simulate NAT/hop latency in the test environment. Palisade to share top-key histograms and VPC diagram. Next sync on 2026-08-18 to review results.
00:52:18 Jared: i'll also send pricing for a Dedicated trial and Private option pros/cons doc.
00:52:25 Marta: thanks, this was productive.

00:57:00 (meeting wrap)
00:57:10 Jared: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and links: -- diagnostics guide: https://console.redwood.ai/docs/diagnostics -- kv hotkey doc: https://console.redwood.ai/docs/kv-hotkeys -- dedicated trial form: https://redwood.ai/trial.
00:57:25 Samir: thanks, bye.
00:57:30 (call ended)
